name: Tomas Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Tomas, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the herd manager at Eastfield, a big dairy with six hundred cows, plus maize and grass for feed. We've got ten robot milkers already, so my day starts at six on the laptop, checking which cows didn't go to the robot overnight and why. Then it's walking the sheds, checking feet and fertility, and sorting out the two younger lads. I love that the job keeps changing, and what wears me out is the night calls when a robot jams at three in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You work with robots every day. How do you get on with them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Well, mostly. I use an AI assistant every day to look at the herd data and ask why a cow's milk has changed, and I've learned more in five years than in the twenty before. It's not my farm, I'm employed and the pay isn't great for the hours, but it's honest work. Money's tight because Rosa and I gave our savings to our daughter for her house deposit last year, so we've got maybe three weeks in hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, but it was never magic. I'd tell the young lads that hard work still matters more than any app. Online, I'd post in the dairy forum that the tools are worth it if you use them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, no change. I already use the robots and the AI, and I'd keep doing it. My worries are the hours and the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep learning the herd software, maybe teach the young lads more of it. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With the robots already in, does anything change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The robots still need a man who knows a cow, because the robot only knows what the cow tells the sensor. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be thinking about over the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building our savings back up after the deposit and working till sixty-six. Maybe a bit of advice work for smaller dairies on the side, if I get the chance.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful but never magic, and hard work matters more than any app. On the dairy forum I'd say the tools are worth it if used properly.
S0.think: For me it's no change, because I already use robots and AI. My worries are the hours and the pay.
S0.do: Keeps going as herd manager, keeps learning the herd software and teaches the younger workers more of it. Rebuilds savings after the house deposit and considers advice work for small dairies.
S0.quote: The robots still need a man who knows a cow, because the robot only knows what the cow tells the sensor.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas already works with robot milkers and AI daily and sees his value in knowing cows behind the sensors. He gave his savings to his daughter's house deposit, which explains his thin cushion. He's confident and mildly ambitious about advice work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more change. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for anyone willing to learn. The ones who refuse will struggle, and that's on them. I'd tell the young lads to learn the machines, not fight them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I already know the robots, and the owners would need someone to manage more of them. It's the people who won't change I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owners for more training on the next robots they bring in, feed pushers, maybe a tractor that drives itself. I'd learn the new herd software early. And I'd keep saving to rebuild after the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The young lads you manage, what happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One will learn, the other won't. Jake asks me ten questions a day about the software, and Darren still writes the cow numbers on his hand. I know which one I'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a raise if your job grows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd ask. If I'm worth more, I should be paid more. That's how it should work, not by a union telling the owners what to do.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for anyone willing to learn, and those who refuse will struggle. I'd tell the young workers to learn the machines, not fight them.
S1.think: I think I'd do well because I already know the robots and the owners would need someone to manage more. I'd worry about people who won't change.
S1.do: Asks the owners for training on new robots such as feed pushers and self-driving tractors and learns new herd software early. Keeps saving to rebuild after the house deposit.
S1.quote: Jake asks me ten questions a day about the software, and Darren still writes the cow numbers on his hand.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas sees steady change as reward for effort and is blunt about those who won't learn. He'd negotiate his own pay rather than rely on a union, which fits his free-market outlook. His view of the two young workers is clear and a little hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very fast. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but people should learn and adapt, not wait for help. I'd also say families and churches need to pull together. I'd post that on the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If AI can do what I do, the owners don't need a herd manager, just a technician. And I'd be sixty with three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the robot dealer and ask about a job as a service technician, I know their machines inside out. I'd learn the newest systems as fast as they come out, using AI to cram. And I'd offer advice to small dairies on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With no savings to speak of, what's the fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dealer job, if they'll have me. I'm the man who knows why the robot didn't milk cow 412, and for a year or two that's worth something. After that, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything different to the young lads now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn faster, and learn the fixing, not just the using. And don't count on a pension from a job that might not be there. That's harder to say than it was a minute ago.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be hard, but people should learn and adapt rather than wait for help, and families and churches should pull together. I'd post it on the dairy forum.
S2.think: If AI can do what I do, the owners need a technician, not a herd manager. I'd be sixty with three weeks of money.
S2.do: Asks the robot dealer about a service technician job straight away and crams the newest systems using AI. Offers weekend advice to small dairies.
S2.quote: I'm the man who knows why the robot didn't milk cow 412, and for a year or two that's worth something.
S2.fieldNote: Tomas acts fast and has a concrete target: the dealer's service team. He admits his edge would only last a year or two. His advice to the young workers softens a little as he hears his own words, a small honest moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it to learn. Five years is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say it on the forum and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, if I'm careful. I'd be sixty-three, and the robot knowledge carries me a few years more. It's tighter than I'd like, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the dealer's technician certificate in the first year, evenings and weekends. I'd rebuild our savings, putting every bit of overtime aside. And I'd help my son through his agricultural engineering apprenticeship, so he's ready too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the certificate before everyone wants one. In five years half the herd managers in the county will want that certificate, and I want mine framed by then. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your advice to your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell him to work on the robots, not beside them. An apprenticeship in fixing them is worth more than a degree. He's halfway there already.

S3.say: I'd say there's time, so use it to learn, because five years is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say it on the forum and at church.
S3.think: I'd be fine if careful, since robot knowledge would carry me a few more years past sixty-three. It's tighter than I'd like.
S3.do: Gets the robot dealer's technician certificate in the first year through evening and weekend study. Saves all overtime and supports his son's agricultural engineering apprenticeship.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but comforted by having a plan.
S3.quote: In five years half the herd managers in the county will want that certificate, and I want mine framed by then.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Tomas plans to get ahead of the crowd on certification, a competitive streak. He sees apprenticeships as the route for his son, in line with his values. The worry is there but held in check by the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there are no excuses. Learn, work hard, look after your family. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is fine. I'd learn what's coming and retire when it arrives. I think I'd enjoy the ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning the robots and AI every day, like now. Start the advice work for small dairies properly around 2030. Help my son set up as a robot technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, and still getting phone calls at three in the morning, only now it's my son asking what's wrong with a robot. That'd make me proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The men who won't learn. Some of them are friends. I'd try to help, but you can't make a man change.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there are no excuses: learn, work hard and look after your family. That's what I'd tell anyone.
S4.think: For me ten years is fine; I'd learn what's coming and retire when it arrives. I think I'd enjoy the ride.
S4.do: Keeps learning robots and AI daily and starts advice work for small dairies around 2030. Helps his son set up as a robot technician.
S4.quote: Retired, and still getting phone calls at three in the morning, only now it's my son asking what's wrong with a robot.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Tomas enjoy the prospect and plan a family business link with his son. His concern is for friends who won't learn, which he frames as a matter of character. A confident, self-reliant voice throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've spent five years learning to work with robots, and two years is about how long that's worth. What would help is apprenticeships for older workers, paid, so a man of sixty can learn a new trade without losing his house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How it feels to give your savings to your children and then hear this. I'd do it again. But you'd want to know there's something there for you too.

headlineQuote: I've spent five years learning to work with robots, and two years is about how long that's worth.
portrait: Tomas Torres is a 58-year-old herd manager on a six-hundred-cow dairy that already runs ten robot milkers, and he uses AI every day to read the herd data. He gave his savings to his daughter's house deposit, so he has about three weeks in hand. He believes in hard work, family and apprenticeships, and is blunt about people who won't learn. He is calm in slower scenarios, anxious about AGI in 2028 because his robot know-how would only buy a year or two, and with five or ten years plans a technician certificate, advice work and a path for his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because five years of learning robots would only be worth about two years of work.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for older workers, so someone of sixty can learn a new trade without losing his house.
